The paper does not compare baselines under this analysis and nevertheless makes broad robustness claims.

Several robustness conclusions are confounded. Environmental-corruption experiments primarily measure the robustness of the upstream MapTRv2 generator, lack competing association methods, and even attribute success to MapTRv2's temporal modeling. Similarly, the nonmonotonic data-efficiency results and near-saturation at 5% are not investigated for sample redundancy or run variance.

Reproducibility currently depends on promised future releases. The manuscript provides no accessible code or dataset artifact, omits the exact OSM snapshot and preprocessing details, and contains conflicting settings such as weight decay 0.05 in the main text versus 0.005 in the appendix. Numerous terminology, citation, and presentation inconsistencies further impede verification.

strengths: The manuscript identifies a practically relevant problem: connecting inexpensive global road maps with locally generated lane maps could enable more current lane-level navigation. The task formulation is intuitive and potentially useful. The proposed OMA benchmark is potentially valuable. It combines OSM and nuScenes, includes clean and perception-generated maps, and evaluates three upstream map generators across Boston and Singapore.

MAT's combination of topological ordering and spatial serialization is well motivated for heterogeneous map alignment. On the authors' benchmark, it improves over all reported baselines while MAT-T runs at 34 ms.

The empirical section is broad, including component and hyperparameter ablations, cross-city transfer, corrupted SD maps, nuScenes-C conditions, data-efficiency experiments, qualitative results, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The central NR P-R metric is not soundly specified. Equation 7 sums rather than averages over thresholds; the text alternates between 10 and 11 thresholds; and, most seriously, validation recall is declared to be one and precision is then reported directly as NR-F1 instead of computing the harmonic mean. Thus identically named validation and test scores represent different quantities. The pseudocode also omits one-to-one matching, tie handling, duplicate predictions, and empty-bin aggregation.

Test performance is extremely sensitive to the arbitrarily selected geometric threshold: MAT changes from 6.6 at 0.5 m to 45.0 at 1 m, 68.2 at 1.5 m, and 72.4 at 2 m. There is no principled threshold justification or evidence that method rankings remain stable. The metric also conflates upstream map-generation quality with association quality, weakening the claimed association comparison.

The baseline study is not sufficiently controlled. Most competitors were designed for trajectory, one-to-one graph, or point matching and their adaptations and tuning are barely described. There is no strong learned map-to-map baseline using the same inputs and training objective; PTv3 appears only in one validation ablation; and the KNN baseline is incorrectly cited to an unrelated 1965 observational-studies paper. No multi-seed variation or statistical testing is reported.

Important algorithmic details are problematic or missing. Path-aware attention enumerates all root-to-leaf paths, which is undefined for cyclic road graphs and can require exponentially many paths; the claimed linear or polynomial complexity therefore lacks support. The appendix's beam-search equations do not impose the stated road-connectivity constraint and rely on conditional probabilities not defined by the association head. The CTC target construction, hierarchical stage transitions, and token-duplication behavior are also unspecified.

The dataset's validity and reproducibility are insufficiently established. The paper claims 2.6M manually annotated lane vectors, yet describes GPS pre-alignment followed by fewer than 1% specialist corrections, without annotator counts, inter-annotator agreement, audit sampling, or clarification of repeated labels in overlapping crops. Low-quality test predictions are excluded without criteria, creating possible selection bias. The annotations and code are only promised after publication.

The evaluation remains geographically and operationally narrow. It uses two nuScenes locations, while validation and test share scenes and differ mainly in whether ground-truth or generated OP maps are supplied. Cross-generator evaluation is useful but does not demonstrate generalization to a genuinely independent dataset, mapping provider, sensor platform, or road system.

The headline claim of achieving lane-level guidance is not directly evaluated. Experiments measure local map association but provide no end-to-end navigation success, route continuity, correct-lane/turn selection, planning benefit, or performance under actual dynamic road changes. Consequently, the safety and deployment claims exceed the evidence.

Several results and implementation details further reduce confidence: data-efficiency performance is non-monotonic and based on apparently single runs; the paper claims semi-supervised potential without a semi-supervised experiment; weight decay is 0.05 in the main text but 0.005 in the appendix; and the full-attention setting is only 2 ms slower than grouped attention, weakening the efficiency motivation.

Novelty is not adequately positioned against map conflation, geospatial graph alignment, and SD-to-HD alignment literature. Spatial serialization appears closely related to Point Transformer V3-style serialized attention, yet PTv3 is not properly cited or discussed, making the architectural novelty difficult to assess. Overall, the promising task and dataset do not outweigh the metric, comparison, technical-specification, and reproducibility problems at a top-tier venue.
